strengths: The paper addresses a relevant question for multimodal NLP: how visual evidence competes with language-based expectations. WHOOPS-AHA! provides a useful diagnostic setup with manually checked candidate continuations and model-specific text-only filtering.

The study combines logit inspection, attention analysis, targeted interventions, and visual-token ablations across two VLMs. The large changes in candidate-token preference and comparatively weak random-head effects provide evidence that the selected components influence this behavior.
Attention-selected visual-token ablations outperform the tested gradient-magnitude and random baselines in Figure 5. The qualitative examples help connect these effects to recognizable image content.
The paper provides dataset-generation prompts, compute information, and an explicit discussion of limitations concerning logit lens, synthetic data, and single-token evaluation.
weaknesses: The central intervention is inconsistently specified. Equations 4–5 make positive lambda amplify counterfactual heads' image attention and suppress factual heads' text attention, whereas Figure 4 describes the opposite. Moreover, the reported range [-3, 3] produces negative post-softmax weights when |lambda| exceeds 1. Such signed interventions can establish sensitivity, but require a different interpretation from simply increasing or decreasing attention. The implementation and results must be reconciled, with controls separating suppression, sign reversal, and activation-scale effects.

The main metric establishes preference between two selected tokens, not successful steering of generated answers. Section 4.3 reports that the factual token's average rank worsens from 3 to 31 at lambda = 3 despite increased 'factual accuracy.' This raises a substantive possibility that the intervention suppresses the competing token while promoting unrelated outputs. Full-vocabulary probabilities, top-1 completions, and systematic generation-quality evaluation are needed; KL divergence from baseline is not itself a measure of grammaticality or correctness.

No held-out evaluation is described for head selection or the choice of 20 heads per group. Selection, tuning, and evaluation appear to use the same roughly 430 examples. The random-head control is useful but uses 100 heads and does not establish matching by layer, modality attention, or output magnitude. Held-out results, matched controls, and uncertainty estimates are needed to substantiate stable conflict-specific specialization.

The mechanistic interpretation exceeds the demonstrated causal evidence. Late heads attending to visual tokens does not establish transmission with 'limited intermediate processing': those representations have already undergone substantial computation. Likewise, zeroing visual embeddings at the transformer input disrupts every downstream pathway and cannot distinguish direct transmission from mediation. Ordinary, non-conflicting visual-grounding controls would also help determine whether the identified heads specifically resolve conflicts or generally convey visual evidence.

The attribution experiments support greater deletion sensitivity than the tested baselines, but do not measure localization precision against annotated regions. Zeroing contextualized visual embeddings is also different from removing image pixels. The claim that a small localized subset drives predictions is substantially clearer for LLaVA-NeXT than Gemma3, whose curve improves gradually over extensive removal. Quantitative region annotations or complementary attribution tests would strengthen the broader localization claim.

Reproducibility and conceptual clarity need revision. Baseline factual preference changes from 27%/24% in Section 4.1 to 22%/18% in Section 4.3 without explanation; exact checkpoints, head identities, and implementation details are insufficiently specified, and the code/dataset footnote has no usable link in the supplied PDF. Furthermore, visually correct descriptions of unusual scenes are repeatedly called 'factually incorrect,' conflating atypicality with falsehood. These issues, together with the intervention and evaluation concerns, prevent a sound Findings recommendation in the current version.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant question for multimodal NLP: how visual evidence competes with language-based expectations. WHOOPS-AHA! provides a focused experimental setting, with manually checked continuations and model-specific filtering to establish text-only preferences.

Experiments on LLaVA-NeXT and Gemma3 combine component-level logit inspection, attention interventions, and visual-token ablation. The substantial changes in pairwise token preference, together with random-head and random-patch controls, provide evidence that the selected components influence the measured behavior.

The attention-based deletion curves outperform the tested gradient baseline in both models. Dataset-generation prompts, compute requirements, qualitative examples, and discussion of logit-lens limitations provide useful methodological context.
weaknesses: The central intervention is inconsistently specified. Equations (4)–(5) increase counterfactual-image attention and decrease factual-text attention for positive λ, whereas Figure 4 describes the opposite. Moreover, the reported range [-3, 3] makes one multiplier negative when |λ| > 1. This reverses contributions rather than merely suppressing attention, and post-softmax scaling also changes attention magnitude without normalization. The actual implementation needs clarification and controls separating modality reweighting from sign reversal and magnitude effects.

The primary outcome does not establish reliable steering of generated answers. 'Factual accuracy' only compares two selected token logits, and Section 4.3 reports that the factual token's average vocabulary rank worsens from 3 to 31 at λ = 3 despite the claimed factual-preference improvement. This permits an apparent success even when neither candidate is likely to be generated. Full-vocabulary probabilities, actual completion rates, and systematic generation-quality evaluation are needed; KL divergence from baseline is not itself a quality metric.

The evidence does not isolate conflict-specific mechanisms from ordinary visual grounding. An unusual scene need not contradict factual knowledge, and describing rainbow hats or fruit in the supplied image is not 'factually incorrect,' as Figure 6 suggests. Without matched nonconflicting scenes or comparable ordinary grounding tasks, the selected heads could be general visual-information heads rather than specialized conflict-resolution components. The narrower finding about competition between textual expectations and visual evidence is better supported.

Head selection, the choice of 20 heads per group, and intervention evaluation appear to use the same dataset, with no reported held-out validation. The random-head control is useful but uses 100 heads rather than a matched selection and does not establish specificity relative to similarly located or similarly image-attending heads. Repeated control samples and uncertainty estimates would strengthen the localization claim.

The spatial and information-flow conclusions exceed the attribution evidence. Zeroing contextualized visual embeddings demonstrates sensitivity to those embeddings, not precise localization of the original pixels or limited intermediate processing. No region annotations support the claimed attribution 'precision,' and only a basic gradient baseline is tested. Figure 5 also shows substantially more gradual changes for Gemma3 than for LLaVA-NeXT, weakening the general claim that a small localized region drives the effect.

Reporting gaps impede reproduction and interpretation. Section 4.1 gives factual-preference baselines of 27%/24%, while Section 4.3 gives 22%/18% without explaining the difference. Exact checkpoint identifiers, component-projection details, and random-control sampling procedures are insufficiently specified; the PDF's code-and-dataset footnote contains no usable link. These issues, together with the intervention ambiguity and outcome-validity concerns, require substantive revision before a sound Findings recommendation.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant NLP question: how vision-language models balance linguistic priors against conflicting visual evidence. WHOOPS-AHA! provides a useful diagnostic setting with rich anomalous scenes, manually checked candidate completions, and text-only filtering.

The analysis combines component-level logit inspection, attention measurements, targeted interventions, and visual-token ablations across two model families. The substantial reported intervention effects, together with random-head controls, provide evidence that the selected heads influence the measured factual-versus-visual preference.

Attention-based patch selection outperforms raw-gradient selection and random removal on the reported deletion metric. The dataset-generation prompts, compute information, qualitative examples, and explicit discussion of logit-lens limitations are useful.
weaknesses: The central intervention is inconsistently specified. Equations 4–5 make positive λ amplify counterfactual image attention and suppress factual text attention, whereas Figure 4 describes the opposite. Moreover, λ outside [-1, 1] produces negative post-softmax weights under these equations. The strongest reported effects therefore involve sign reversal rather than simply increasing or decreasing attention. This does not invalidate intervention evidence, but the implementation must be clarified and nonnegative interventions tested before interpreting the results as controlled reweighting of information sources.

The main outcome measures pairwise token preference rather than successful output steering. Section 4.3 reports factual preference increasing substantially while the factual token's average vocabulary rank worsens from 3 to 31. Thus, the intervention may suppress the competing token without making the intended continuation likely. Full-vocabulary prediction rates, candidate probability mass, and systematic generation evaluation are needed. KL divergence from baseline and a few captions do not establish preserved generation quality.

The experiments do not sufficiently distinguish conflict-specific mechanisms from ordinary visual grounding. Unusual scenes can legitimately override typical textual continuations; describing an depicted rainbow hat is not factually incorrect. Matched non-conflicting scenes and ordinary visual questions would help establish whether these heads specifically mediate knowledge conflict. Likewise, attention to visual positions in late layers does not establish 'limited intermediate processing,' because those representations have already undergone substantial computation.

Head selection, the choice of 20 heads per group, and evaluation appear to use the same small dataset; no held-out evaluation is reported. This limits evidence that the identified roles generalize across examples. The random-head control is helpful, but lacks reported repeated sampling and matching for layer, intervention magnitude, or baseline visual attention. Uncertainty estimates and held-out head-selection experiments would strengthen the localization claim.

The attribution evidence supports deletion sensitivity more directly than spatial precision or a direct information pathway. Zeroing contextualized visual embeddings can disrupt general visual information, and no annotated-region localization metric or matched factual-image control is provided. Figure 5 also shows a much more gradual response for Gemma3, weakening the general claim that a small localized region drives predictions. The superiority claim should be restricted to the tested raw-gradient baseline and deletion metric.

Reproducibility and reporting require important corrections. Baseline factual preference changes from 27%/24% in Section 4.1 to 22%/18% in Section 4.3 without explanation. Exact checkpoint identifiers, inference templates, head-level projection and normalization details, and random-control settings are insufficiently specified; the code/dataset footnote has no usable link in the supplied PDF. Together with the intervention ambiguity, these concerns prevent a clear Findings recommendation, although a focused revision could reasonably address them next cycle.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant question in multimodal interpretability: which model components mediate competition between linguistic priors and visual evidence. WHOOPS-AHA! provides a useful, focused setting with explicit alternative completions.

Experiments on LLaVA-NeXT-7B and Gemma3-12B combine logit inspection, targeted interventions, visual-token ablations, and localization analysis. The large changes in pairwise token preference provide evidence that the selected heads causally influence this behavior.

The paper includes meaningful supporting controls: random-head interventions, random-patch ablations, POPE evaluation, and experiments on Visual CounterFact. The localization analysis reports paired statistical tests, and the appendices provide dataset-generation prompts and human validation.
weaknesses: The central claim of a dedicated conflict-resolution mechanism exceeds the evidence. Unchanged POPE accuracy after suppressing selected heads establishes only that this intervention does not affect that particular binary task. It does not exclude general visual retrieval, task-specific readout, or redundant processing. Matched factual and counterfactual images with identical completion prompts are needed to establish conflict specificity. Late-layer attention also does not establish that visual information undergoes limited intermediate processing.

The strongest steering results are difficult to interpret as ordinary modulation of attention. Equations 1–2 produce negative post-softmax weights when |λ| exceeds 1; at λ = 3, counterfactual image contributions are multiplied by −2. Such interventions can demonstrate causal influence, but sign reversal and changes in activation magnitude confound the interpretation as balancing information sources. Report nonnegative interventions, separate interventions on each head group, and controls matched for layer and intervention magnitude.

The principal metric compares only two selected logits, so increased 'factual accuracy' need not mean that the model actually generates the factual answer. Appendix F reports that the factual token's average vocabulary rank worsens from 3 to 31 at λ = 3, precisely where factual preference is strongly increased. This directly limits the behavioral-control claim. Full-vocabulary probabilities, top-1 completions, and systematic generation-quality evaluation are needed; two caption examples and KL divergence do not resolve this concern.

No held-out protocol is described for selecting heads, choosing their number, and evaluating intervention efficacy. Selecting extreme heads and optimizing their count on the evaluated examples can overstate stability. Visual CounterFact re-identifies heads on the new dataset rather than testing the original fixed heads; overlap is encouraging but does not establish intervention transfer. Held-out evaluation and fixed-head transfer would materially strengthen the findings.

The attribution evidence supports a narrower conclusion than precise identification of conflict-inducing regions. The object-mask comparison uses only 20 images and SAM3-generated masks without reported human verification. LLaVA-NeXT's median ratio improvement over gradients is modest, 2.05 versus 1.88. Zeroing contextualized visual embeddings measures sensitivity to representation removal, which is not equivalent to removing image pixels or isolating an anomalous object's causal role.

Reproducibility and reporting need improvement. Important details are unspecified, including exact model checkpoints, handling of words split into multiple tokenizer tokens, logit-lens normalization and head-output projection, and the gradient aggregation rule. Gemma3's baseline factual preference is reported as both 24% and 18%. Dataset validation is also limited: human–LLM exact agreement on factual alignment is only 35% on 20 entries, weakening the claim of uniformly reliable commonsense priors.

Overall, the paper presents promising causal sensitivity results, but important revisions are needed to substantiate its defining claims about conflict specialization and reliable output steering. These are evidence and interpretation concerns, rather than a lack of subjective novelty or interest, and prevent a sound Findings recommendation in the current form.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant question in multimodal interpretability: how visual evidence competes with text-induced parametric priors. WHOOPS-AHA! provides a useful, focused setting for token-level analysis.

The experiments go beyond correlational attention visualization. Targeted head interventions and visual-token ablations demonstrate causal influence on the measured factual-versus-counterfactual preference in both LLaVA-NeXT and Gemma3, with substantially weaker effects from random controls.

The supplementary experiments add meaningful evidence: replication on Visual CounterFact, substantial overlap between independently selected heads, and a POPE control. These support some robustness of the observations, although their interpretation needs qualification.

Attribution evaluation includes both deletion experiments and quantitative object-mask comparisons. Table 4 reports paired significance tests for both models, providing stronger support than qualitative examples alone.
weaknesses: The central claim of a dedicated conflict-resolution mechanism is not established. Unchanged binary POPE accuracy after suppressing selected heads only establishes a null effect on that particular task and intervention. It does not distinguish conflict sensitivity from specialization for particular concepts, answer tokens, or completion formats. A matched comparison using ordinary and anomalous images with the same prompts and answer vocabulary is needed. Likewise, late-layer attention to image-token positions does not establish 'limited intermediate processing,' because those representations have already undergone substantial computation.

The strongest steering results have a problematic interpretation. Equations 1–2 modify post-softmax weights without stated renormalization, and the chosen range extends to ±3. For λ > 1, counterfactual image weights become negative; for λ < −1, factual text weights become negative. These interventions reverse and rescale contributions rather than simply weaken attention. Figure 4's largest gains occur in this regime. Moreover, Appendix F reports that the factual token's average vocabulary rank worsens from 3 to 31 at λ = 3. Thus, improved pairwise 'factual accuracy' need not mean the model actually generates the factual answer. Absolute probabilities, full-vocabulary predictions, and separate suppression/amplification controls are necessary.

Head selection and evaluation are not clearly separated. The paper reports selecting heads and choosing their number on the analyzed dataset without documenting a held-out protocol. Visual CounterFact re-identifies heads on that dataset, so it demonstrates replication of the procedure rather than direct transfer of the original intervention. The observed head overlap is encouraging, but frozen-head transfer and held-out evaluation would provide stronger evidence. Random controls should also match head count, layer distribution, and intervention assignment, with variability across draws.

Several quantitative inconsistencies undermine confidence in the reported results. Section 5.1 gives Gemma3's multimodal factual accuracy as 24%, whereas Section 5.3 gives an 18% baseline. At λ = 3 and 20 heads per group, Figure 10 appears to show roughly 55% for LLaVA-NeXT and 62% for Gemma3, rather than Figure 4's approximately 74% and 83%. Figure 10 also continues improving beyond 20 heads despite the accompanying claim that performance peaks there. Different settings or populations could explain these discrepancies, but none are specified.

Reproducibility is incomplete despite the provided prompts and compute information. The manuscript does not adequately specify exact model checkpoints, prompt/chat formatting, treatment of single words that tokenize into multiple subwords, the precise per-head logit projection, or gradient aggregation. The first-page code/data marker has no usable link in the supplied PDF. These details materially affect token-level analyses and should accompany executable evaluation code and the selected head indices.

The attribution findings are promising but narrower than the broad superiority claim. Mask evaluation uses only 20 images and SAM3-generated masks without a described human verification procedure. The LLaVA-NeXT median advantage over gradients is modest (2.05 versus 1.88), despite statistical significance. Comparison with raw gradient magnitude supports superiority over that baseline, not gradient-based attribution methods generally. Zeroing contextualized visual embeddings also establishes dependence on those representations, not necessarily a direct causal pathway from localized image pixels.

The operationalization conflates typicality with factual truth: an unusual scene can be accurately described even when its completion is unlikely from text alone. Consequently, increasing 'factual accuracy' can reduce image-grounded correctness. This does not invalidate the controlled preference experiment, but it limits claims about hallucination and reliability. Overall, the paper contains useful empirical observations, but the mechanistic overclaims, intervention interpretation, and unresolved reporting discrepancies require important revisions before a sound Findings recommendation.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant question for multimodal NLP: how visual evidence competes with strong textual priors. WHOOPS-AHA! provides a useful, controlled completion setting with model-specific checks that the text-only input favors the commonsense answer.

The analysis goes beyond correlational attention visualization. Targeted interventions shift factual-versus-counterfactual token preferences in both LLaVA-NeXT and Gemma3, with random-head and MLP controls providing additional evidence that the selected heads have causal influence.

The attribution results combine patch ablation, qualitative examples, and quantitative object-mask comparisons. Appendix I reports paired significance tests and results for both architectures, supporting the narrower claim that the selected heads localize relevant visual evidence better than the tested gradient baseline.

The Visual CounterFact experiments and substantial overlap between independently identified head sets strengthen the evidence that the observations are not unique to WHOOPS-AHA!. The paper also provides generation and evaluation prompts, human validation, and compute information.
weaknesses: The central claim of a dedicated conflict-resolution mechanism exceeds the controls. Unchanged POPE accuracy after suppressing selected heads establishes limited necessity on one different task; it does not establish selective recruitment under conflict. POPE differs in answer vocabulary, prompt structure, and visual demands, and redundant visual pathways could preserve accuracy. Matched factual/counterfactual images with the same completion task, together with layer- and visual-attention-matched head controls, would better distinguish conflict resolution from ordinary visual evidence retrieval.

The strongest intervention effects are difficult to interpret as improved reliance on factual knowledge. Under Equations 1–2, values of |λ| above 1 reverse the sign of some post-softmax attention weights rather than simply suppressing them. Such interventions can demonstrate causal influence, but need separate interpretation from natural modality weighting. More importantly, Appendix F reports that the factual token's average vocabulary rank worsens from 3 to 31 at λ = 3 despite improved pairwise 'factual accuracy.' Full-vocabulary predictions, absolute target probabilities, and quantitative generation-quality results are needed to establish behavioral steering rather than a change in ordering between two increasingly unlikely answers.

The paper does not describe a held-out split for selecting heads, choosing their number, and evaluating interventions. Appendix G re-identifies heads on Visual CounterFact rather than directly testing transfer of the original head set. The overlap is informative, but frozen-head evaluation on unseen examples would provide stronger evidence of a stable, generalizable mechanism.

Several numerical inconsistencies undermine confidence in the reported effects. Section 5.1 gives a Gemma3 factual baseline of 24%, whereas Section 5.3 gives 18%. Figure 10, explicitly evaluated at λ = 3, shows substantially lower performance at 20 heads than Figure 4 at the same stated setting, and performance continues increasing beyond 20 heads despite the claim that 20 maximizes accuracy. These discrepancies need reconciliation.

Reproducibility details remain incomplete despite the useful appendices. Exact model checkpoints, inference templates, treatment of words spanning multiple tokenizer tokens, head-output projection/normalization, gradient aggregation, and random-control repetitions are not specified adequately. The supplied PDF's 'Code and Dataset' marker has no resolvable link. These details materially affect token-level mechanistic measurements.

Dataset and localization validation are encouraging but limited: human evaluation covers only 20 examples, with 35% exact agreement for text-only knowledge alignment; localization uses 20 SAM-generated masks without reported human verification. Typical completions also need not represent factual necessities, so following an unusual image is not itself a hallucination. Overall, the paper supports a promising narrower contribution, but unresolved measurement, reporting, and causal-specificity concerns prevent a clear Findings recommendation.
